My first experience with the found phone game genre was disappointing. I found [I]Replica[/I] to be an undercooked, preachy, borderline sciolistic game that is best not played. My excitement for this genre was quashed quickly, but I remembered that I still have [I]SIMULACRA[/I] in my backlog of games. Because of that, I decided to give found phone games another try.

Coincidentally, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] was partly inspired by [I]Replica[/I] (as seen by the titles), and partly by [I]Her Story[/I], one of my favourite games of all time. I loved [I]Her Story[/I] for its intriguing narrative and presentation, so I had some hope for [I]SIMULACRA[/I]. Thankfully, after my disheartening first exposure to found phone games, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] did not disappoint.

[I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a mystery game, in which you find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna. By digging deep into her personal life chronicled by the contents of her phone and Internet activities, you uncover clues as to why Anna had gone missing. The puzzles in this game are fun, fair, and hardly difficult. Because of that, the game manages to present the story in a nice flow. It also helps that [I]SIMULACRA[/I] has a slick presentation, with a clean, Android-like user interface that controls well with mouse and keyboard. The in-game videos are pretty well done, too, but I did find the voice acting for one particular character to be laughable.

Despite [I]SIMULACRA[/I] being described or classified as a horror game, I did not find it scary.  Aside from a few instances, in which some players may find the game's version of a "jump scare" frightening, I considered this game to be more suspenseful. You can feel the plot thickening and tension building as the game progresses, with some subtle (but usually not so subtle) graphical and audio alterations making the game increasingly unnerving. The way [I]SIMULACRA[/I]'s story unfolds is almost Hitchcockian.

As much as I enjoyed the game narrative, I did find the ending slightly abrupt. It seemed like there is more story to tell, and perhaps the spin-off game, [I]SIMULACRA: Pipe Dreams[/I], may tie up some loose ends. Still, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a very enjoyable game, made even better if played in the dark with earphones on. The developers smartly included a "Begin+" mode that will unlock after the first playthrough. This mode allows you to replay the entire game with sped-up text, so you can retry certain scenarios without needing to sit through the slow, deliberate pace of the chat sessions. (It's also a time saver for achievement hunters.) [I]SIMULACRA[/I] gets an enthusiastic recommendation from me.

P.S.: I wrote this review after completing [I]Sara is Missing[/i] the predecessor of this game. [I]SIMULACRA[/I] shares many similarities with [I]S.I.M.[/I] (Coincidence? I think not!), and [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is clearly more refined in both story and game mechanics. Both games are worth playing, as they are both good ambassadors for the found phone game genre.

Thankfully, after my disheartening first exposure to found phone games, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] did not disappoint. [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a mystery game, in which you find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna. By digging deep into her personal life chronicled by the contents of her phone and Internet activities, you uncover clues as to why Anna had gone missing. The puzzles in this game are fun, fair, and hardly difficult. Because of that, the game manages to present the story in a nice flow. It also helps that [I]SIMULACRA[/I] has a slick presentation, with a clean, Android-like user interface that controls well with mouse and keyboard. The in-game videos are pretty well done, too, but I did find the voice acting for one particular character to be laughable. Despite [I]SIMULACRA[/I] being described or classified as a horror game, I did not find it scary. Aside from a few instances, in which some players may find the game's version of a "jump scare" frightening, I considered this game to be more suspenseful. You can feel the plot thickening and tension building as the game progresses, with some subtle (but usually not so subtle) graphical and audio alterations making the game increasingly unnerving. The way [I]SIMULACRA[/I]'s story unfolds is almost Hitchcockian. As much as I enjoyed the game narrative, I did find the ending slightly abrupt. It seemed like there is more story to tell, and perhaps the spin-off game, [I]SIMULACRA: Pipe Dreams[/I], may tie up some loose ends. Still, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a very enjoyable game, made even better if played in the dark with earphones on. The developers smartly included a "Begin+" mode that will unlock after the first playthrough. This mode allows you to replay the entire game with sped-up text, so you can retry certain scenarios without needing to sit through the slow, deliberate pace of the chat sessions. (It's also a time saver for achievement hunters.) [I]SIMULACRA[/I] gets an enthusiastic recommendation from me. P.S.: I wrote this review after completing [I]Sara is Missing[/i] the predecessor of this game. [I]SIMULACRA[/I] shares many similarities with [I]S.I.M.[/I] (Coincidence? I think not!), and [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is clearly more refined in both story and game mechanics. Both games are worth playing, as they are both good ambassadors for the found phone game genre.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is an interesting horror game where the events unfold through a phone screen.

Story:

You play as an unnamed man/woman. We find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna, we find a message of her begging for help and well we launch into an investigation to figure out how to save her.

The story in Simulacra is quite intriguing and all the research you do to figure out what happened to Anna and all the people around her, is quite interesting, because you go through many sites, reading articles and text messages, most of it having some decent writing behind it.

Graphics:

Well the only graphics in this is your phone. The phone has it's own OS named Iris and it's styled after an android phone. It looks quite convincing. You definitely know what each app represents so the art team definitely nailed the look of a smart phone.

Audio:

The acting is pretty sub-par, the actress that plays Anna is the only one that is semi-decent, but everyone else does a pretty mediocre job. However where the game shines the most is in it's audio design. The noises you hear around you when you browse the phone send a shiver down your spine. It could be something simple, like a small whisper to a creepy silent laugh. 

Gameplay:

Simulacra is mostly a puzzle solving game, where you have goals and you have to figure out how solve and these puzzles have a pretty decent design. A liked quite a few of the puzzles and how fresh they felt.

These puzzles range from pretty simple to sometimes head scratching. But it never felt cryptic and actually quite a few of the puzzles required a really logical solution and it felt like it would be something I would do in real life. 

You can do a bunch of research by reading articles, reading text messages so there's a lot of stuff to do in the phone. Also not to mention there's multiple choices throughout the story and multiple endings for you to achieve. 

Verdict:

Simulacra is a pretty unique horror game and it's story is pretty intriguing. With multiple endings and a really interesting plot I loved my time with this game and honestly I suggest giving it a shot at full price.

Pros:
+ Story is pretty intriguing
+ Nails the look of a smartphone perfectly
+ Multiple choices lead to different outcomes and endings
+ Great puzzles

Cons:
- Acting is not good whatsoever 

Final Rating:
8.5/10

My first impression from the game was very good - creepy glitchy visuals here and there, atmospheric sound effect, possibility of creeping into strangers phone (yeah I am stalker af so whatttt) and putting random pieces of information together to uncover the story. Awesome, I love games like this!

If it would stop there, it would be so good, but the story is unfortunately ruined by terrible, unsatisfying conclusion, and all that build-up atmosphere just vanishes and you stare at the screen like "are you kidding me Mr. Developer couldn't you think of something even cheesier" and you can't help but think about your high school essays where you couldn't think of proper ending of a story so you just shoved some aliens in there and hoped nobody would care.

Anyway the premise and execution are still quite good and I am fully aware that my opinion of the story can be just my personal preference.

review_text_raw:
A rather short game about a missing person.

You work on the missing persons mobile phone throughout the game and interact with Apps and send messages to persons.
While doing so, through music and ambient sounds, and a scare from time to time, this game creates an extremely intense atmosphere and pulls you into it's world!

Very, very good game. Highly recommend playing it. The 4€ are not much to pay for a couple hours of enjoyment!

I played it for a bit more than 5h now in one day.
In this time I completed my first and therefore truthful to my character playthrough, with a rather satisfying, though not "good" ending.
This took me around 4-4.5h

The remaining time, and time that will add from now on, is used for achivements, since this game let's you have them rather easily by reaching certain optional objectives that are never stated anywhere though ;)
So if you like to get into some secret hunting: This might be a game for you!

At the time of writing this review, I completed 4 out of 5 endings.
All of which are different enought to have their own twist to them! Really nice.

I know what the last ending will result in, but the details are yet unknown.

There are some negative points though, as no game is perfect.

Since we are talking about a "mobile game port" (to my knowledge that is), there are some essentials lacking.

This game features no settings menu of any kind.
It is not possible to lower the audio, except through the OS' sound mixer ...
That is not acceptable, far less in a post TB (TotalBiscuit) world.
Being able to lower Sound, Music and/or Video (which is sparsely used), would make this a more proper PC-game.
Also I haven't seen the possibility to change resolution, though the game is played only on about 10% of the screen anyway (due to the type of game it is ...)

There are subtitles hidden in the help-menu in main menu.

Especially in the later part of the game, the music is a tad too loud in comparison with the voices, so understanding suffers from it.

Other than the just stated? Not much to complain about.
Scrolling is a bit awkward, but works well enough by mousewheel and "dragging" via left click.
Typing in the places necessary is a bit lackluster since backspace deletes the whole last word (which can be a pain for fast typers that want to correct a misstype ...)

THats pretty much it.
Support this awsome dev!

A phone is left on your doorstep. Like the kind stranger you are, you unlock it to start looking for the owner, but it becomes obvious really quickly that something is wrong...

Multipe endings also give it replayability.

This is fine for the most part, you basically work with them for the greater good to find Anna, but what kind of pissed me off was that you [spoiler] HAVE to be nice to Taylor and trust him to unlock the only good ending. This guy is NOT trustworthy [/spoiler]

Still had a BLAST with it and would reccomend playing it!

7.5/10

I don't know how I missed this one when it first came out. I've played a couple of these titles that have you navigating a lost phone (A Normal Lost Phone, Another Lost Phone: Laura's Story, Replica, etc.), and generally find the premise captivating, even if I have some irritations with the details of each game. In addition, SIMULACRA was quite well received on Steam. At the time of this writing, the game has 96% positive reviews overall!

As I began to explore, there was a lot to like about the game. The phone felt "real," and I thought that the Apps that were present were a good reflection of what many young people have installed. I enjoyed the "de-scramble" puzzles that allow you to decrypt texts and photos, although a few of the text puzzles seemed like they should have multiple solutions. Lastly, I thought that the sound design was brilliant. Periodic background sound effects keep the player tense and worried about their exact location while perusing the phone's contents. Lastly, the sound effect recorded by Greg in Anna's home (also used later in the game) is just so unnerving. The game does an excellent job of creating an unsettling tone.

But of course, there were a number of things I didn't like as well. I felt that the game could be a bit too linear during the majority of the playthrough - you often were forced to have dialogue with either Greg or Taylor before the game would progress, even if you weren't particularly interested in talking with them. I thought it felt strange to receive calls on the phone and be unable to answer. Afterwards, the caller would typically ask you by text why you didn't answer, and you typically would respond with something like, "I couldn't understand what you were saying." However, I never felt that I had difficulty understanding what was said - the game just didn't provide me with the means to respond. Lastly, I just wasn't particularly impressed with the videos of Anna. Perhaps the actress was asked to adhere too closely to a script, but her video blogs did not feel very organic to me.

Luckily, I found the final act of SIMULACRA to be absolutely fascinating. I want to refrain from spoiling the game for anyone, but the game has something important to say about conformity and romantic desirability in the digital age. Real life has a "messiness" that can easily be omitted in our curated digital worlds. Do we lose our humanity through this omission? What if we did?

review_text_raw:
This game has a pretty powerful story. A very GOOD one at that. 
If you take the time to go through everything, read everything, pay close attention. you can expect at least a good 5-8 hours of gameplay, It sucks you in out of curiosity. 
The choices you make may not be the best one even if you think it is. honestly i almost cried a little at the end if not at the same time a bit horrified.  

Throughout the gameplay there had been several moments of intense psychological fear, that is, pending on your definition of what "fear" is to you, this game will absolutely Tap into your Head one way or another!
The unknown is what makes you curious & dig deeper, you will have choices of extreme moral dilemmas, it will make you question yourself. it will make you question others, you'll think twice and three times more. with multiple endings, multiple choices, there are many ways to play this game, there are many directions to go and it may not play out the same as you might see on others game plays such as you tube etc. 

 The best part of the entire game was the build up, terrifying sounds that had me literally shaking & taking a break for a good 10 minutes, there are moments of silence and sudden disturbing yet harmless interruptions. 

Overall, between the puzzles & stumped moments, frights, jump-scares, humor etc, there is NOTHING i didn't like about this game. 
I HIGHLY recommend purchasing it & i HIGHLY recommend playing it more than once!  The devs did a spectacular job building this game based on Simulacrum, Simulation & Hyperreality.  bravo.

now that it's complete, I need to sit in a fetal position & think about what I've done.
PS. keep a pen & paper with you.  it will come in handy
